Advenient had outgrown its identity. The old look felt generic in a crowded field of digital marketing companies. The task was to build more than a new logo: a recognizable and cohesive identity that reflected the team’s work, personality, and ambition.

I personally led the project from client communication through design. The client wanted teal and orange because they felt this combination differentiated Advenient from other digital marketing companies. I focused on creating a legible, recognizable mark around their idea of growth and extending it into a cohesive brand system.
Lead client communication, logo development and design applications.
Use a caret (^) as a simple exponent-inspired symbol for growth while keeping the logo distinctive and readable.
Build the approved teal-and-orange identity across print, social and team materials through collaborative revisions.

I personally led client communication and the branding process. The original brand guide also credits Valentin Jose Adrian Bonite (project management), Harriette Haw and Coleen Yuson (brand strategy), and Harriette Haw, Leandro Miguel B. Tupas and Coleen Yuson (identity/application design).

The client wanted the logo to symbolize growth. To make that idea simple and immediately recognizable, I used a caret (^)-a symbol commonly used to express exponents-as the foundation of the mark. Its connection to exponential growth gave the identity a meaningful starting point.

The real design challenge was balancing readability with recognition: the mark needed to be easy to understand while clearly feeling like Advenient. The final orange symbol could sit alongside the wordmark, stand alone as an icon, or become a repeatable element within layouts.
Concept study: the exponent-like form stands for growth and forward movement.
Construction and positioning of the signature Advenient brandmark.

Before settling on the identity, I considered gradient treatments, a different logo concept and alternative color directions. An earlier logo direction did not resonate, which made the need for a clear, recognizable mark even more important.

The client was firm about using teal and orange. In their view, the pairing stood apart from what other digital marketing businesses were using. Rather than push a different palette, I worked within that preference and focused the exploration on making the symbol both legible and distinctively Advenient.
These earlier directions are described from the project process; rejected concepts are not shown as approved final artwork.
Variations explore the mark as a flexible graphic device.
Alternative executions while maintaining core brand recognition.

The guide includes the approved primary wordmark, single-color and outline treatments, and a stand-alone brand symbol. I developed each to retain the upward exponent gesture while adapting to different backgrounds and applications.

The brand symbol can also stand alone when the full name is not required. These individual marks were exported from the vector artwork pages in the source brand guide rather than cropped from a presentation mockup.
Primary two-tone wordmark: verdigris lettering with the warm orange exponent mark.
Solid orange brand symbol, built around an upward exponent.
The outlined mark explores contrast between the orange form and verdigris border.
Orange outlined version for alternate uses.

The brand guidelines define four values-freedom, growth, adventure and balance-and a design approach that is minimalist, fun, fresh and new. The visual system keeps those ideas tangible through strong color, straightforward shapes and consistent typography.
Verdigris teal and warm orange anchor the identity. A wider palette offers contrast and variety where needed, while DM Sans keeps everything legible, from oversized headlines to smaller body text.
Black / Bold / Regular. A single flexible family for headlines, subheads and body copy.
See the palette and typography in the guide

DM Sans creates continuity across scale and hierarchy.

The identity guidelines do more than show attractive applications: they specify how the logo should be handled. The mark must remain upright and aligned to the logotype, and the secondary arrangement places the symbol after the wordmark.

The guide also documents what to avoid: stacked lockups, gradients applied inside the symbol, distortion, and off-palette two-tone combinations. A dedicated exclusion-zone diagram demonstrates how clear space protects the logo in use.
Correct and incorrect logo treatments from the original identity guide.
The exclusion-zone specifications keep the mark legible across contexts.
Once the identity direction was established, the client and I worked closely on tangible brand applications, particularly business cards, staff IDs and ID slings, alongside social and print designs.

I developed around two to three revisions per design, balancing the client’s requests with my recommendations. The system was refined across formats without making every layout identical; the guidelines also documented logo use and clear-space rules.

blocks.text: KOTA Center Davao is a nonprofit community center focused on supporting young boys through growth, learning and community. The project was to create a recognizable visual identity and, crucially, a social media system the organization could continue using after my involvement ended.

KOTA needed more than a logo: it needed a media style guide and adaptable social templates that its team could use independently. The client wanted red to remain central and the organization’s culture to be respected, without borrowing Indigenous visual motifs simply for decoration.

A few days after meeting the client, I revisited a book they had given me for inspiration and noticed the Grand Cross emblem. That night an idea came to me in a dream: part of the motif resembled a K. I used that shape as the starting point for the logo, then built a red-led identity and reusable social templates around it.

I developed the logo and social media identity system in direct collaboration with the client at KOTA Center Davao. The client reviewed the work and guided decisions about cultural representation and the red palette.
A symbol with a reason to exist.

During an early meeting, the client handed me a book they thought might help with inspiration. I remember it being about saints, although I am not certain. While skimming the book I noticed a visual from the Grand Cross badge. Later that night, the direction came together in a dream: a detail of the emblem looked like the letter K.

I used that K-like detail as the foundation of the mark. As documented in the original guide, the symbol also lends itself to readings of a flag and an open door-ideas connected to identity, belonging and welcome. This gave KOTA a usable visual foundation without leaning on borrowed local ornament.
KOTA Center Davao primary identity: a compact red symbol and clean wordmark.

The first directions raised an important question: how do you make a brand feel connected to Davao without using familiar cultural imagery as a shortcut? The client felt some of the initial ideas leaned too heavily on local culture.

We specifically did not want to use Indigenous designs of Davao merely for branding. I decided to pivot away from those directions rather than force cultural motifs into a logo that did not need them.

The Grand Cross detail gave me another route. Its K-like shape was legible, adaptable and distinctive, which let the identity carry KOTA’s name and purpose more directly. The final decision came from discussion and revisions with the client, not from the visual reference alone.
Build a recognizable KOTA logo using a letter-like detail from the Grand Cross motif.

Give KOTA a practical style guide and social templates that other team members could continue to use.

The client wanted red to remain the main brand color. Working with red, white and the geometric Poppins type family gave the identity a recognizable foundation and made event information, headlines and announcements easier to organize consistently.

I extended the K-shaped geometry into flexible image frames and layout elements. The goal was not to lock KOTA into one composition, but to give future contributors a system they could recognize and reuse.

I created the social media style guide and reusable layouts so the KOTA team could continue producing branded content after I was no longer needed for every post. This included Facebook page and event covers, 1:1 square posts and Instagram Stories.

The final work brought together the logo, color palette, typography and a social media style guide with reusable Facebook, event, square-post and Instagram Story layouts. I wanted the system to remain useful when the organization made content without me.

The client responded very positively to the identity and told me how good it felt for KOTA to finally have one. That feedback matters to me because the goal was not only an attractive mark but something they could recognize as their own.

As far as I have observed, KOTA’s Facebook page has continued to use the identity, although its appearance has evolved as other people have taken over creating posts. This continued use is a meaningful outcome of the handoff; it is not a claim that I designed those later posts or that the identity produced measurable engagement gains.

I designed applications across Facebook covers, social posts, business cards, signage and menus. Each touchpoint needed to carry the same recognizable Wünderbar identity whether it appeared online, in a printed piece or at an event.

Wünderbar is a mobile pop-up bar created to bring European-inspired cocktails and social rituals into Davao’s events and gatherings. Its founding story combines a love for local community with experiences of Mediterranean cafés and northern European pubs.

Wünderbar wanted a recognizable visual identity for bringing European-inspired drinks to events in the Philippines. I was hired to design the brand and its applications, with a visual direction that could feel connected to European drink culture and still work across social media, menus, business cards and signage.

I explored 21 logo variations to give the client a meaningful range of options. Gothic typography supported the European-inspired concept, and the cocktail-stirring spoon tied the symbol to the actual drinks. The client chose the navy-and-gold palette; we ultimately agreed on the same preferred logo without major pushback.

I created the brand identity and collateral directly with the client, who collaborated with me on creative direction and final selection. The cocktail illustrations used in the menus were made by another creative and are not credited as my own illustration work.

Wünderbar was conceived as a mobile bar bringing European-inspired drinks to events and gatherings in the Philippines. The client wanted an identity that felt connected to this concept rather than a generic nightlife brand.

I chose Gothic-inspired lettering because it felt appropriate to both the client’s vision and the European aesthetic behind the business. The cocktail-stirring spoon became a distinctive motif directly connected to the act of making drinks.
The chosen logo combines Gothic-inspired lettering with the cocktail-stirring spoon motif.
I prepared 21 logo variations for the client. That number was intentional: I wanted to show what the brand could become and give the client genuine options before choosing a direction.

Throughout the project, creative direction was collaborative. I handled the identity design work, while the client helped shape the vision and determine what fit the business best. Gothic lettering and a cocktail-stirring spoon became the combination that felt true to the European-inspired concept.

There was no dramatic disagreement over the final logo. The client loved the chosen direction, and it was the same one I wanted to see selected. That shared decision made the final identity feel natural rather than forced.
Selected designs from the 21 logo variations prepared for the client to compare.

The final logo combines Gothic-style lettering with a cocktail-stirring spoon-the tool I chose to connect the identity to making drinks. The small text DVO, MMXXV and PH references Davao, 2025 and the Philippines.

The navy-and-gold direction came from the client. I brought those colors together with Gothic-style display typography and clean DM Sans supporting text, so the brand could be expressive in the logo and still remain readable across menus and social graphics.

This document outlines the design

designer's ability to align with the brand’s

tHE BRAND STORY
Ingenuity Software isn’t just another tech 
firm—we are architects of precision, crafting 
software that is as refined as it is powerful. Our 
foundation is built on years of expertise, but 
our vision is future-focused: to redefine what 
it means to deliver world-class digital 
solutions. Every product we create is designed 
with intent, balancing sophistication with 
innovation, and ensuring longevity in an 
ever-evolving industry. More than a service 
provider, Ingenuity is a premium 
experience—trusted by those who value 
quality, expertise, and exceptional 
craftsmanship.

The Ingenuity logo embodies the company’s 
commitment to endless possibilities, 
innovation, and adaptability, aligning with its 
six foundational pillars. Its refined design 
reflects movement, resilience, and strategic 
thinking, reinforcing the company’s ability to 
evolve and break boundaries.
The updated modern typeface enhances this 
vision by offering a sleek, contemporary look 
that balances boldness with versatility. This 
change ensures the logo remains timeless, 
highly legible, and adaptable across various 
applications, solidifying Ingenuity’s position as 
a forward-thinking and dynamic brand.

inspection_method.Drive catalog: All descendants of the confirmed folder were enumerated through the connected Drive account. Path segments preserve the exact source names. Dates printed on projects are distinct from file modification dates.
inspection_method.Source group: A Drive file’s association with a project establishes its containing folder. It does not establish that every revision, photograph or linked item is Yancy’s work or selected for the website.
inspection_method.Standalone source links: Matching basenames identify candidates for the corresponding web artwork. These candidates have not been verified as identical pixel content across codecs or edits.
inspection_method.Web images: Each listed image URL was fetched in the public portfolio context, decoded, measured in pixels and hashed from its delivered bytes. Appearances identify its owner from a project page, index link, homepage link or a project-specific image reference.
inspection_method.Originals: Pixel dimensions come from file headers when available. Vector dimensions keep their literal units. A full-file SHA-256 is present only after the entire binary was read. Archive catalog entries without deeper inspection are labeled by their recorded MIME type and path.
inspection_method.PDF copy: Text is retained by 1-based PDF page where available. Some headings and graphics exist only in artwork. Project page prose preserves published wording with whitespace normalized. Personal contact data inside original artwork should be checked before future publication.
